bio.en: Keith Rabois is a veteran operator and investor, part of the PayPal Mafia, and an early backer of Stripe, Palantir, Airbnb, YouTube, DoorDash, Ramp, and many others.
bio.zh: 基思·拉博伊斯（Keith Rabois）是一位资深运营者与投资人，属于"PayPal 黑帮"成员，并早期投资了 Stripe、Palantir、Airbnb、YouTube、DoorDash、Ramp 等数十家公司。

summary.en: Keith shares contrarian takes, including that the traditional product manager role makes less sense as AI handles more building and that founders should rarely talk to customers directly. He argues the modern PM skill is increasingly CEO-like - defining what to build and why. The episode is full of sharp, provocative views on talent, org design, and leveraging AI.
summary.zh: 基思分享了许多反共识观点，包括：随着 AI 承担更多构建工作，传统的产品经理角色意义变小；创始人不应亲自去和用户交谈。他认为，现代 PM 的技能越来越像 CEO——定义要构建什么以及为什么。本期充满关于人才、组织设计与运用 AI 的犀利而具挑衅性的见解。

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: ... idea of a PM makes no sense in the future. The skill is more like being a CEO now, which is what are we building and why?
turns.zh: ……未来产品经理这个概念已经没有意义了。现在这种能力更像是当一名 CEO——也就是我们到底在构建什么、为什么而构建？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a lot of anxiety in the job market.
turns.zh: 就业市场里弥漫着大量焦虑。

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: AI is going to radically reorient lots of people's careers and maybe including mine. What I've noticed in some of the best organizations is the number one consumer of tokens is the CMO. They don't need to rely upon deputies and deputies and deputies to get actual work product.
turns.zh: AI 将从根本上重塑很多人的职业生涯，或许也包括我自己的。我在一些最优秀的组织里注意到的一点是：消耗 token 最多的，其实是 CMO（首席营销官）。他们不再需要层层依赖副手才能拿到真正的工作成果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to hit on some contrarian takes that you have. Your advice you don't actually want to be talking to customers.
turns.zh: 我想聊聊你的一些反共识观点。比如你有个建议是：你其实根本不该去跟客户交谈。

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: I hate talking to customers. I refuse to allow colleagues of mine to talk to customers.
turns.zh: 我讨厌跟客户交谈。我也拒绝让我的同事去跟客户交谈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You have this idea of criticizing in public versus in private.
turns.zh: 你有个「公开批评」与「私下批评」的区分理念。

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: High performance machines don't have psychological safety. They're about winning.
turns.zh: 高绩效的机器不需要心理安全感。它们的全部意义在于赢。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You're uniquely great at helping companies build world-class teams.
turns.zh: 你最独特的过人之处，是帮助企业搭建世界级的团队。

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: If a founder shows the ability early in his or her career to assess talent ruthlessly and accurately, here's how you can go very far with no other abilities whatsoever.
turns.zh: 如果一个创始人在职业生涯早期就展现出冷酷而精准的识人能力，那么即便他毫无其他本事，也能走得很远。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It feels like it's never been harder to attract the best talent.
turns.zh: 如今吸引顶尖人才，似乎从来没有像现在这么难。

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: Really talented people. When things are going well, they're not happy. The morale actually does go down when people are skating. The single role for the CEO is offsetting that complacency. The better you're doing, the more the CEO should push.
turns.zh: 真正有才华的人，当事情进展顺利时反而并不开心。人们混日子的时候，士气其实是在下滑的。CEO 唯一的作用，就是抵消这种自满。你做得越好，CEO 就越该往前推。

Before we get into it, don't forget to check out lennysproductpass.com for an incredible set of deals available exclusively to Lenny's newsletter subscribers. With that, I bring you Keith Rabois. turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: It's a pleasure to be with you.
turns.zh: 很高兴来到这里。

turns.speaker: Lenny

turns.zh: 好，我们刚开始录音时你告诉我，你是用 iPad 来录这期节目的，而我从来没用过 iPad。你还分享了一个惊人的事实——你已经好几年没碰过电脑了。聊聊这是怎么回事吧。

I haven't touched a computer since September 2010. Everything I do in my life is either done from my phone, my watch, or my iPad.
turns.zh: 对。我刚去 Square 工作时，Jack Dorsey 就是用 iPad 在运营公司的。所以我立刻在 2010 年 9 月也换了过来，从此没回头。自 2010 年 9 月起我就没再碰过电脑。我生活里的一切，要么用手机，要么用手表，要么用 iPad 完成。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's so interesting about this as you were talking is just there's this trend of engineers starting to code from their phone, at Boris Cherny on and Simon Willison, these two engineers that are 10X engineers, and they're just coding from their phone talking to AI. And I feel like you've been preparing for this for a long time.
turns.zh: 你刚才说这些的时候，我觉得特别有意思的一点是：现在出现了工程师开始用手机写代码的趋势，比如 Boris Cherny 和 Simon Willison——这两位都是十倍工程师——他们就直接用手机跟 AI 对话来写代码。我感觉你好像为此已经准备很久了。

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: Yeah. I'm trying to be ahead of the curve. Jack's very good at being ahead of the curve. If you just watch what Jack's doing and follow, you're in pretty good shape in technology.
turns.zh: 对，我尽量走在曲线前面。Jack 就很擅长走在前面。你只要看着 Jack 在做什么、跟着做，在科技圈就能处于相当不错的状态。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And just to understand the benefit, is it just avoid distractions?
turns.zh: 我只是为了搞清楚它的好处——就是为了减少干扰吗？

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: Yeah, partially distractions, partially just the flexibility. Taking an iPad with you anywhere is just super easy. Some laptops have improved since then, but the screen flexibility, angles, but just the weight. I carry my iPad with me everywhere. There's nothing you can't perform unless maybe if you're doing heavy duty engineering, which obviously has not been my forte in life, although I may have to start. There's no reason to use a more powerful, heavier weight, less flexible machine.
turns.zh: 对，一部分是减少干扰，一部分纯粹是灵活性。带着 iPad 去任何地方都超级轻松。这些年有些笔记本确实有进步，但无论是屏幕的灵活性、角度，还是重量，都不如它。我走到哪儿都带着 iPad。没什么事是它做不了的——除非你做的是重度工程开发，那显然不是我人生的强项，虽然说不定我以后也得开始做。既然如此，根本没有理由去用一台更强、更重、更不灵活的机器。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. iPad Maxing, Keith Rabois.
turns.zh: 哇。Keith Rabois 的「iPad 极限使用」。

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: See if you got my Apple. As long as it's an Apple product, it works.
turns.zh: 看你能不能 get 到我的苹果梗。只要是苹果的产品，就行。

I want to focus on something that I think you're uniquely great at, which is helping companies build world-class teams. And I want to start in particular with attracting the best talent. (00:05:11): And what's really interesting these days, from what I can tell, is there's just a lot of people that are struggling to find a job. It's taking a lot longer to find a job. It's just there's all these layoffs. On the other hand, it feels like it's never been harder to attract the best talent. There are so many amazing companies doing amazing things, so much money flying around, these hundred million dollar offers and things. (00:05:32): And so from the companies that you are closest to that you see are best at attracting the best talent, what have they figured out? What are they doing differently? What are some creative things they do?
turns.zh: 这太应景了。本期节目由我们本季的主赞助商 WorkOS 呈献。OpenAI、Anthropic、Cursor、Vercel、Replit、Sierra、Clay，以及成百上千其他成功的公司，它们的共同点是什么？它们全都由 WorkOS 驱动。如果你在做面向企业的产品，一定体会过集成单点登录、SCIM、RBAC、审计日志，以及大公司要求的其他功能时的痛苦。WorkOS 用一个专为 B2B SaaS 打造的现代化开发者平台，把这些成交障碍变成了即插即用的 API。(00:04:14)：说真的，我作为投资人投的每一家开始向上拓展市场的初创公司，最后都用了 WorkOS，因为它们就是最好的。无论你是想拿下第一个企业客户、还在种子期的初创，还是正在全球扩张的独角兽，WorkOS 都是让你具备企业级能力、解锁增长的最快路径。它本质上就是企业级功能的 Stripe。访问 workos.com 开始使用，或者直接去它们的 Slack 找人——那里有真正的工程师随时等着回答你的问题。WorkOS 让你用令人愉悦的 API、详尽的文档和顺滑的开发者体验更快地构建。今天就访问 workos.com，让你的应用具备企业级能力。(00:04:52)：我在准备这次对话时，发现这个话题可以展开的方向实在太多了。你在太多事情上都极其聪明。我想聚焦在你最独特擅长的那件事上——那就是帮助企业搭建世界级的团队。而我特别想先从「吸引最顶尖的人才」说起。(00:05:11)：从我观察到的情况来看，如今真正有意思的是：有大量的的人在艰难地找工作，找到工作花的时间比以往长得多，到处都是裁员。但另一方面，吸引最顶尖的人才似乎又从未如此困难。 有那么多厉害的公司在做厉害的事，那么多钱在流动，还有上亿美元的报价之类的。(00:05:32)：那么，在你最亲近、也最擅长吸引顶尖人才的公司里，它们想通了什么？它们做对了哪些不同的事？有哪些有创意的做法？

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: Well, let's start with first principles. The most important lesson I learned when I was working at Square from my board was Vinod Khosla was on my board, and he said, "The team you build is the company you build." And that adage is the most important thing when you're creating a startup. People get distracted with the market, with customers, with a product, with technology. Ultimately, it's the team. If you have the right people, everything else will be easy and you have the wrong people, everything else is going to be difficult. (00:06:11): So, Vinod distilled it, but I actually learned this back on my PayPal days. So in the early 2000s, why was PayPal so successful? Why were there subsequent generations of successful, interesting companies for 25 years now? It's because Peter Thiel and Max Levchin marshaled an incredible density of talent. So it allowed PayPal to succeed where possibly we wouldn't have. And these people went on with interesting ideas, ambition, and talent to build epic companies in all kinds of verticals. (00:06:45): So from day one, day one of my technical career, technology career, I've always been focused on the importance of critical density talent, how do you identify, retain, and promote people with that talent? Back in the PayPal days, when I first started my career in technology, I actually truthfully was not very good at this. Fortunately, Peter and Max were. So Max basically hired all the technical talent in the organization. Peter pretty much hired everybody else. They used their network primarily. So it was very difficult to get a job at PayPal, unless you had a first degree or second degree connection to the engineering team or to Peter through Stanford. (00:07:24): Which is a different type of recruiting model. It works really well if you have a strong network. I wouldn't recommend it for everybody, but if you have a network that has unique talent, there's no substitute. Interviews are not a great substitute regardless of how strong you are at interviewing. But when I started my career, I was mediocre at let's say hiring people, probably 50/50. Some good people, some mediocre people. That doesn't allow you to scale a team with an unfair advantage. (00:07:53): But what I learned to do is steal people from other people's organizations within PayPal very successfully. So I got feedback from David Sachs, who was the COO at the time that I wasn't going to get promoted again until I could demonstrate leverage, leadership leverage, which he had an equation for of one plus one has to equal three or more. So for every incremental person you hire, you have to show that you produce disproportionate returns, non-linear returns. (00:08:18): And because I wasn't hiring that well, I wasn't really succeeding at that leverage. So when I went around, took the feedback into account, I said, "Okay, I really want to get promoted. What do I do?" So I found people within the organization that I felt had talent that were not being leveraged to the highest potential inhibition, and I recruited them to my team. And that was very successful. (00:08:42): And then I did get promoted actually fairly quickly because these people actually left to speed. They were able to run really fast and we produced a lot of really important results for the company. The lesson though that I took away was, well, that's great because what it showed to me is I actually could identify talent. I just couldn't identify strangers with talent. So people that were in the building that I have lunch with or dinner with or go for a runaround the PayPal campus with, I was accurate at diagnosing their abilities. I just couldn't do it in a 20-minute, 30-minute, 45-minute interview. (00:09:15): So the first thing is just double down on people I know. That doesn't scale perfectly, but learn to be excellent at, if I had context, assessing people's abilities, superpowers and weaknesses. Then over the next X years, tried to identify a different technique for identifying, assessing random people. Because ultimately if you're going to build an organization, ultimately if you're going to be a VC, you can't just invest in people that you already know. So that took some years and required some training. (00:09:47): Anyway, I think you can teach some of this to a founder, but one advantage a founder has that's going to thrive is if a founder shows the ability early in his or her career to assess talent ruthlessly and accurately, here's how you can go very far with no other abilities whatsoever. Hiring is like a muscle. You need to exercise it. You need to try, learn what worked, what didn't, what could you have known, what did you miss, why, and riff on that and try to get better at it. (00:10:20): There are tactics you can learn. I think the tactics work pretty well within the middle of a bell curve distribution of moving yourself 10, 20 degrees within that bell curve. I don't think the tactics can really teach you how to identify, call it top 10 basis points, top 50 basis points of talent. There you have to deviate from the norm. And I think that's actually true of most lessons in life. (00:10:41): If you're going to be extraordinary in any skill, you can't follow a playbook. Otherwise, by definition, lots of other people would be the top 10 basis points, but you can get a lot better by learning techniques. So for example, let's share a couple. (00:10:55): One thing I think you can learn to do is be excellent at references. It doesn't work for hiring people right out of college or something because the reference context is going to be a little off, but I think without getting better at interviewing and assessing, if you just learn to extract the right information from ruthless referencing. So for example, ruthless referencing to me means Tony at DoorDash does 20 references on every single senior hire, 20.
turns.zh: 好，我们先从第一性原理说起。我在 Square 工作时，从董事会学到的最重要的一课，来自时任董事的 Vinod Khosla，他说过一句话：「你搭建的团队，就是你搭建的公司。」这句话是创业时最重要的事。人们会被市场、客户、产品、技术分散注意力。但归根结底，是团队。如果你有对的人，其他一切都会变容易；如果你用错了人，其他一切都会变难。(00:06:11)：Vinod 把它提炼成了这句话，但其实我早在 PayPal 时期就学到了这一点。在 2000 年代初，PayPal 为什么能那么成功？为什么在此后的 25 年里，会有一代又一代成功而有趣的公司延续下来？因为 Peter Thiel 和 Max Levchin 聚集了一批密度惊人、极其出众的人才。正是这样，PayPal 才得以在我们原本可能失败的地方取得成功。而这些人后来带着有趣的创意、野心和才华，在各个垂直领域建起了伟大的公司。(00:06:45)：所以从我的技术生涯、职业生涯的第一天起，我就一直专注于「关键密度人才」的重要性——你如何识别、留住并提拔具备这种才华的人？在 PayPal 年代，我刚踏进科技行业时，说实话我在这件事上并不擅长。幸好 Peter 和 Max 擅长。所以基本上所有技术人才都是 Max 招的，其他人大体上都是 Peter 招的。他们主要用的是自己的人脉。所以在 PayPal 拿到 offer 非常难，除非你跟工程团队有直系或隔代的关系，或者能通过斯坦福搭上 Peter 的关系。(00:07:24)：这是一种不同的招聘模式。如果你有强大的人脉，它效果非常好。 我不会把它推荐给所有人，但如果你的人脉里确实有独特的人才，那没有任何替代方案。面试并不是好的替代方式，无论你面试能力多强。但我刚入行时，招人水平顶多算平庸，大概一半对一半——招到过一些好人，也招到过一些平庸的人。这根本无法让你带着不对称优势去扩张团队。(00:07:53)：但我后来学会了一招，就是从 PayPal 内部其他人的团队里「挖」人，而且非常成功。当时 COO David Sacks 给了我一个反馈：在我能证明自己的杠杆、领导杠杆之前，我不会再被提拔——他有一个公式，即一加一必须等于三或更多。也就是说，你每多招一个人，都必须证明你带来了不成比例、非线性的回报。(00:08:18)：因为我当时招人水平不行，在杠杆这件事上其实没做成功。于是我反思了这个反馈，心想：「好吧，我真的很想被提拔，那我该怎么办？」于是我在组织内部找到了一些我认为有才华、但潜力没有被充分释放的人，把他们招进了我的团队。结果非常成功。(00:08:42)：后来我确实很快得到了提拔，因为那些人真的开始加速运转。他们跑得飞快，我们为公司产出了大量极其重要的成果。但我从中吸取的教训是：这很好，因为它向我证明，我其实是有能力识别人才的。我只是没法识别「陌生人」里的人才。所以对于就在公司里、能一起吃饭、一起跑步的人，我判断他们的能力很准。只是在 20 分钟、30 分钟、45 分钟的面试里，我做不到这一点。 (00:09:15)：所以第一件事，就是在我认识的人身上加倍下注。这并不能完美地规模化，但要学会一件事：在了解背景的前提下，精准地评估一个人的能力、超能力和弱点。然后在接下来的若干年里，我尝试找到另一种方法来识别和评估陌生的人。因为归根结底，如果你要搭建一个组织，如果你要做一个 VC，你不可能只投资你已经认识的人。所以这件事花了我好几年，也需要一些训练。(00:09:47)：总之，我觉得其中的一部分可以教给创始人，但一个能成功的创始人所具备的优势是：如果他在职业生涯早期就展现出冷酷而精准的识人能力，那么即便他毫无其他本事，也能走得很远。招聘就像一块肌肉。你需要去锻炼它。你需要去尝试，去总结哪些做对了、哪些没做对、你本可以知道什么、你漏掉了什么、为什么，然后在此基础上调整，努力做得更好。(00:10:20)：有一些技巧是可以学的。我认为这些技巧在钟形曲线的中段很管用——能让你在曲线内部挪动 10 度、20 度。但我并不认为这些技巧能教你如何识别，比如说，前 10 个基点、前 50 个基点的顶尖人才。在那里，你必须偏离常规。我觉得人生中大多数道理都是如此。(00:10:41)：如果你要在任何一项技能上做到卓越，你就不能照搬剧本。否则按定义，会有很多其他人也处在前 10 个基点的位置。但你可以通过学习方法来变得好很多。所以举个例子，我们分享几个吧。(00:10:55)：有一件事我觉得你可以学会，就是把「背景调查」做到极致。 对于刚毕业的大学生这类人，这招不太管用，因为背景参照会有些偏差；但我认为，即便不提升面试和评估能力，只要你学会从「无情的背景调查」里提取正确的信息，就足够了。比如对我来说，「无情的背景调查」意味着：DoorDash 的 Tony 对每一个高层招聘都会做 20 份背景调查，20 份。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: I bet you he's pretty good and that he's been pretty accurate too. So I think you can learn that. That's a skill that's teachable, that being absolutely incredibly dedicated to your craft, you can just get better at. Back in the day, there's an investor at Greylock who's on my board at LinkedIn, David Sze, very successful investor, notable for both LinkedIn and Facebook investments. He used to teach at Greylock, you couldn't stop referencing a founder until you hit a negative reference. So you would know you had exhausted the reference when you finally hit a negative reference. (00:12:02): And so I think there are tactics there in muscle building. How do you get the right information from the right people? How do you frame the questions, et cetera? That will lead you in the right direction. Now, you have to be careful, let's say, I'll give you an example where this can go wrong. (00:12:18): I've been a longtime investor from the seed round of a company called Faire, founded by two of my colleagues at Square, Max Rhodes and Jeff Colvison worked for me at Square and then the two other co-founders also worked at Square. When people were reference checking Max, often most VCs asked the wrong question, which was, "Was Max a good employee?" The answer to that is very mixed. (00:12:43): And so some venture capitalists, including some very good ones, were nervous about investing in Faire. If they frame the question slightly differently, which is, "Is Max capable of being a world-class entrepreneur?" the answer was yes. So again, it's a tactic you have to understand, what exactly am I trying to extract? Same person, wrong question, wrong result. And many people passed on Fire and they regret it. And these are actually quite talented investors. They just didn't frame the question correctly when they were calling someone like Jack Dorsey up for the reference.
turns.zh: 我敢打赌他做得很好，而且一直以来都很准。所以我认为这是可以学会的。这是一种可以被传授的技能——只要你对你的手艺绝对、惊人地投入，你就能越做越好。早年间，Greylock 有一位投资人 David Sze，也是 LinkedIn 时期我董事会的成员，他是非常成功的投资人，以投资 LinkedIn 和 Facebook 闻名。他在 Greylock 时有个规矩：在找到一条负面评价之前，你对一个创始人的背景调查就不能停。所以当你终于挖到一条负面评价时，你就知道自己已经把背景调查做透了。(00:12:02)：所以我认为，在训练这块肌肉方面是有方法可循的。你如何从对的人口中得到正确的信息？你如何措辞提问？这些都会把你引向正确的方向。当然，你也得小心——我给你举一个会出错的例子。(00:12:18)：Faire 这家公司，我从种子轮起就是长期投资人，它由我在 Square 的两位同事创办——Max Rhodes 和 Jeff Colvison 都曾在我手下工作，另外两位联合创始人也都在 Square 干过。当初大家给 Max 做背景调查时，很多 VC 问了一个错误的问题：「Max 是个好员工吗？」这个答案其实很模糊。(00:12:43)：所以一些风投，包括一些很厉害的，都对投资 Faire 感到犹豫。如果他们把问题略微换一种问法——「Max 有没有能力成为一个世界级的创业者？」答案就是肯定的。所以，这又回到了那个方法：你必须清楚自己到底想挖出什么信息？同一个人，问错了问题，就得到错误的结果。很多人因此错过了 Faire，现在都后悔莫及。而他们其实都是相当有才华的投资人。他们只是在给 Jack Dorsey 这类人打电话做背景调查时，没把问题问对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Any other questions you find really helpful in extracting the right information?
turns.zh: 还有哪些问题，是你觉得在提取正确信息方面特别有用的？

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: When I interview candidates for senior people in leadership positions, I always ask them, look at whatever company they're at and say, "If you were CEO, what would you have done differently?" And you get a feel for their strategic mindset of can they drive value creation? Because almost by definition, they've come from a company that's had some traction success, so can they edit? So in your case, I would've asked you, "If you were CEO of Airbnb, what would you have done differently?" And you learn a lot from that question. (00:13:49): On references specifically, I think a general arc that's pretty good is asking the person, what would lead to this person being most successful? And if something were not to work out, what would be the primary root cause that you can identify if something going wrong? I think generally probing on those two arcs leads to a lot of insight.
turns.zh: 当我面试高层领导岗位的候选人时，我总会让他们看着自己所在的公司说：「如果你是 CEO，你会做出哪些不同的决策？」这样你就能感受到他们的战略思维——他们能不能驱动价值创造？因为几乎按定义，他们来自一家已经取得一定成功的公司，所以他们懂不懂得「编辑」？所以换作是你，我就会问：「如果你是 Airbnb 的 CEO，你会做出哪些不同的决策？」你能从这个问题里学到很多。(00:13:49)：具体到背景调查，我觉得一个相当好用的通用思路是问对方：是什么会让这个人取得最大的成功？如果事情最终没成，你能指出的根本原因会是什么？我认为，沿着这两条线去深挖，通常能带来很多洞见。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And that first question is for the candidate or is that in the reference?
turns.zh: 那第一个问题，是问候选人的，还是用在背景调查里的？

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: Yeah, for the candidate. That's for the candidate specifically.
turns.zh: 对，是问候选人的。那个是专门问候选人的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it.
turns.zh: 明白了。

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: Because I don't want them to criticize Airbnb. I don't think that's that productive, but you can tell how much of the current business model have they absorbed, how much do they understand trade-offs. And then can they create an unfair advantage? Because they have insights into afterburners. And then I have a follow-up question, which is usually gold, which is, let's say I asked you this question about Airbnb and you give me this great answer. I'm like, "Well, why weren't you able to persuade Brian to do it?"
turns.zh: 因为我不想让他们去批评 Airbnb。我觉得那没多大建设性，但你可以看出他们吸收了多少当前的商业模式，有多理解其中的取舍。然后，他们能不能创造出不对称优势？因为他们掌握着内部的洞察。接着我还会追问一个通常很关键的问题——比如我问了你这个关于 Airbnb 的问题，你给了我一个很棒的回答。我就会说：「那好，你为什么没能说服 Brian 去做这件事呢？」

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So you made this interesting point that there's tactics that can help you get better at finding and identifying talent. A lot of this is just the feedback loop of doing it a bunch, it sounds like. I find the feedback loop is so, it's hard to actually ... Most people interview, hire, and then don't really learn much from how it ends up going. There's this gut thing that happens, but they're not really thinking about it. Do you have any advice for just how to make the most out of the lesson of seeing how something went?
turns.zh: 你提了一个很有意思的点：有一些技巧能帮你更好地发现和识别人才。听起来，这很大程度上就是反复实践形成的反馈循环。我觉得这个反馈循环真的很难……大多数人面试、招人，然后并没有从最终结果中学到多少东西。他们靠的是某种直觉，但并没有真正去思考它。你有没有什么建议，能让人最大限度地从「看结果如何」这个过程中学到东西？

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: So I've read some research on the topic. And if you ask yourself 30 days after any hire, "Would you make the same decision?" That 30-day loop is pretty useful and it basically it's as accurate as measuring in a year or two years out. So you get a pretty tight feedback loop and you can ask the entire hiring team. So I think that is just a technique that every company should use.
turns.zh: 我读过一些关于这个话题的研究。如果你在招人 30 天之后问自己：「我还会做同样的决定吗？」这个 30 天的循环其实非常有用，而且它基本上和用一两年时间去衡量一样准确。这样你就得到了一个相当紧凑的反馈循环，而且你可以让整个招聘团队都来回答。所以我认为，这就是每家公司都应该使用的一个方法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to talk about this framework that you have, barrels and ammunition, because this is really mind-expanding and helping people understand who to even hire.
turns.zh: 我想聊聊你提出的那个框架——「炮管与弹药」（barrels and ammunition），因为它真的非常开脑洞，能帮人想清楚到底该招谁。

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: So look, most companies raise money, they have some traction, they do a seed round, they get launched, they get some traction. Then they raise a lot of money, whether it's a series A or a Series B. And then they hire a lot of people infallibly or at least historically. (00:15:55): And then the CEO, almost without accession, gets frustrated because they've hired a lot of people. The burn rate has increased a lot and they don't feel like more is getting accomplished per unit of time, per day, per week, per month, per quarter, and they get frustrated. And so then they sit around at a dinner with other CEOs or people like me or one-on-one conversation with me and are incredibly unhappy and disappointed that I'm spending all this money on all these people, but we're getting less done or the same done. And why, why, why, why? (00:16:22): After years of sitting through these conversations at dinner with other CEOs or COOs, I realized that the fundamental driver of this is that the number of people that can independently drive an initiative from beginning, from inception to success is very limited within any company. And if you hire more people without expanding the number of what I call burials that can drive from inception to success, all you're doing is stacking people behind the same initiatives. And so you're wasting time, energy, and increasing your collaboration tax, your coordination tax. And so that's what causes the drag coefficient. (00:17:04): So for example, at PayPal, we had about 254 people in Mountain View when we were acquired. Of those people, depending on how strict you really want to be. And this is considered one of the best talent rich networks of all time in technology, there's between 12 to 17 barrels in the organization. That's an infinite number. (00:17:23): I once asked Jack Altman on a podcast at Loudouns, which is a pretty damn big company, how many barrels of the company? The answer was two. That's a more common answer for a very good company. So you have between two and let's say 15 barrels at a company. That defines the unique number of things you can do in parallel versus sequentially. And just hiring more people is not going to change that. And if anything, it's just going to cause a collaboration, a coordination tax, and you're going to have a track revision, you're going to do less. (00:17:50): So the key is to me is if you want to do more or need to do more, your market requires you to do more, your business model requires you to do more, VCs require you to do more, you need to have more barrels. Now, the question is how and when and all this. There's a lot of details there, but fundamentally, the ratio of barrels to ammunition is what dictates the number of important initiatives that can be pursued simultaneously.
turns.zh: 你看，大多数公司融资、有了一些吸引力、做一轮种子轮、发布产品、再获得一些吸引力。然后它们会融一大笔钱，无论是 A 轮还是 B 轮。接着，它们几乎无一例外——或者说至少历史上如此——会招一大批人。(00:15:55)：然后 CEO 几乎不可避免地会感到沮丧，因为他们招了很多人。burn rate（烧钱速度）大幅上升，但他们并不觉得单位时间、每一天、每一周、每一月、每一季度里完成了更多事，于是他们就沮丧了。于是他们会坐在其他 CEO 或我这样的人旁边吃晚饭，或者跟我一对一聊天，无比郁闷和失望地说：「我把所有钱都花在这些人身上了，可我们完成的事反而更少了，或者跟以前一样。到底是为什么、为什么、为什么？」(00:16:22)：多年来，我听了很多 CEO、COO 在饭桌上的这类抱怨，后来我意识到，背后的根本原因是：在任何一家公司里，能够独立把一个项目从零开始、从头带到成功的人，数量都非常有限。而如果你在没增加我所谓「炮管」（barrels，能从头带到成功的人）数量的情况下招了更多人，你只是在同样的项目后面堆更多的人罢了。这样一来，你就是在浪费时间、浪费精力，并且增加了协作税、协调税。而这，就是造成拖累系数的原因。(00:17:04)：举个例子，PayPal 被收购时，我们在山景城大约有 254 人。在这批人里——取决于你想把标准定得多严——而 PayPal 被视为科技史上最顶尖的人才网络之一——整个组织里大概只有 12 到 17 个炮管。这已经是一个极高的数字了。 (00:17:23)：有一次我在 Loudoun 的一档播客上问 Jack Altman——那是一家相当大的公司——「你们公司有多少个炮管？」他的答案是两个。对于一家非常优秀的公司来说，这反而是更常见的答案。所以一家公司大概只有 2 到 15 个炮管不等。这个数字决定了你能并行、而非串行去做的独特事项的数量。单纯招更多人并不会改变这一点。甚至说，那只会带来协作税、协调税，让你不停地返工，结果反而做得更少。(00:17:50)：所以对我来说，关键在于：如果你想做更多、或者市场/商业模式/VC 逼着你必须做更多，那你就需要更多的炮管。至于如何、何时等等，里面有很多细节；但从根本上说，炮管与弹药的比例，决定了你能同时推进多少重要的项目。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And you're not saying you don't want ammunition. It's valuable. To make an impact, you need ammunition in addition to the barrel.
turns.zh: 而你并不是说你不需要弹药。弹药是有价值的。要产生影响力，除了炮管，你还需要弹药。

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: Yeah, you definitely need ammunition. And it depends on what kind of project. There are types of projects where an individual barrel may be able to succeed with very limited or no ammunition. Sometimes you may need a designer, an engineering team, a PM, a data analysis, blah, blah, blah. Depends on what the project is, what the problem you're trying to solve is, what's the proper amount of ammunition? But once you think about the ratios of ammunition to the problem, you can be much more constructive and deliberate and intentional about the team construction.
turns.zh: 对，你绝对需要弹药。这取决于项目类型。有些项目，一个单独的炮管就能在极少甚至没有弹药的情况下成功。有时你可能需要设计师、工程团队、PM、数据分析师，等等等等。取决于这是什么项目、你想解决的是什么问题，以及合适的弹药量是多少。但一旦你开始从「弹药与问题的比例」这个角度去思考，你在搭建团队时就能更有建设性、更审慎、更有意识。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Most people hearing this assume they are barrels. What helps you understand if someone's truly a barrel?
turns.zh: 听到这番话的大多数人，都会默认自己就是炮管。那你怎么判断一个人真的是炮管？

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: Can they take an idea and make it happen? Basically, we're going up that, there's a hill over there, that's the hill. Get us over that hill. And one way or the other, they will motivate people if they need to, they will accumulate resources if they need to, they will measure what they need to, and they're going to get your company across that hill. That's a barrel. Anything less than that is not a barrel.
turns.zh: 他们能不能把一个想法变成现实？打个比方：那边有座山，那就是我们要翻越的山。带我们翻过那座山。无论用什么方式，如果需要，他们会去激励人；如果需要，他们会去攒资源；如果需要，他们会去衡量。总之他们一定会带着公司翻过那座山。这就是炮管。达不到这个标准的，就不是炮管。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so this is skills like internal org stuff, resource. It's the collection of all the things to get something done.
turns.zh: 所以这涉及的是像内部组织、资源整合这类能力。它是一系列把事情做成所需能力的集合。

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: A collection of all those things, so it's basically there's an outcome. CEO, founder wants an outcome and come hell or high water, this person is going to deliver that outcome. Then the outcome can be fairly narrow and not that difficult in the beginning. And then you expand the scope, the complexity, the difficulty that you basically entrust to your barrels. (00:19:59): And sometimes they have no line of sight of how to solve it when you start. Sometimes you have a preliminary idea. So it ranges, but ultimately it's that skill of, I'm going to take this off your plate, you can fire and forget, and this is going to happen. And if it's not going to happen, I'm going to come back to you proactively with the issues I'm confronting, what I've already tried, the diagnosis of the root causes and ask for your help with sufficient time for you to intervene and try to brainstorm with me to get us to the right answer.
turns.zh: 是一系列这类能力的集合，所以本质上就是：有一个结果。CEO、创始人想要一个结果，而这个人无论如何都要把这个结果交付出来。最初，这个结果的范围可以相当窄、难度也不大。然后你再逐步扩大你托付给炮管的范围、复杂度和难度。(00:19:59)：有时在开始时，他们并不知道该怎么解决；有时你有一个初步的想法。情况各有不同，但归根结底就是那种能力：「我会把这事从你肩上接下来，你可以放手不管，它一定能成。」而如果它成不了，我会主动回来找你，带着我所面临的问题、我已经试过的办法、对根本原因的剖析，并在还有足够时间让你介入、和我一起头脑风暴找到正确答案的时候，来寻求你的帮助。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Agency is the word that comes to mind when you talk about this role.
turns.zh: 说到这个角色，我脑子里冒出的词是「能动性」（agency）。

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: Yeah, I think agency is accurate. The problem I have with terms like agency is it's a little bit like strategy. It goes in one ear, a lot of people and out the other ear and they don't really process the meaning.
turns.zh: 对，我觉得「能动性」是准确的。我对这类词的不满在于，它有点像「战略」——从一只耳朵进，又从另一只耳朵出，很多人并没有真正消化它的含义。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Who are some examples of barrels that make this real so people can understand what you're talking about?
turns.zh: 对。能不能举几个真正的炮管的例子，让听众能具体地理解你在说什么？

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: I talked to my YC lecturer in 2014 about how to operate. They can be as simple as the now somewhat famous in technology smoothie test, which is, we used to have engineers work pretty hard at Square and pretty late. And I always wanted them to have food so they wouldn't be famished, they wouldn't be distracted. And I didn't really want them to eat junk food because I actually think junk food's bad for you, bad for your brain, et cetera. So settled on delivery and really wanted to provide a 9:00 PM cold smoothies. (00:21:23): And we had, at that time, a pretty substantial team at Square, office team, EAs, this was not a lean, mean organization. And so I tried through the office team EAs and nothing ... We never got healthy, delicious, and cold smoothies delivered at 9:00 PM. Just kept that one. I was getting frustrating because if the smoothies aren't cold, then no one's going to eat them. If they don't arrive at 9:00, then no one can really bank on their refreshments. Everything went wrong. (00:21:57): And then I had this intern named Taylor Francis, and I was explaining just my frustration. It was his second day at work. And he's like, "I'll solve it." And I was like, "Okay, kid, good luck with that." I was like, "Sure, keep trying." Anyway, day goes by, 9 o'clock arrives. And lo and behold, smoothies show up at 9:00 PM, delivered on the standing desk table where the engineers would congregate. I sample them, they're cold, they taste great. And I'm like, "Oh my God, I found a barrel." And I later gave him almost everything to do.
turns.zh: 我在 2014 年跟 YC 的学员讲过如何运营。炮管可以简单到——就是现在科技圈有点出名的那个「思慕雪测试」。当时在 Square，工程师们经常干得很晚很拼。我总想让他们有东西吃，这样他们不会饿肚子、也不会分心。而我其实不希望他们吃垃圾食品，因为我觉得那对身体、对大脑都不好。所以我决定了用配送的方式，而且真的很想在晚上 9 点提供冰镇的思慕雪。(00:21:23)：那时 Square 有一个相当庞大的团队，有行政团队、EA（行政助理），根本不是一个精简到极致的组织的。于是我试着通过行政团队和 EA 去办这事，结果……我们从来没能成功在晚上 9 点把健康、美味又冰镇的思慕雪送到。就这一件事，一直没成。我越来越 frustrated，因为如果思慕雪不冰，就没人会喝；如果 9 点没送到，大家就指望不上这份加餐了。一切都搞砸了。(00:21:57)：后来我有了一个叫 Taylor Francis 的实习生。我当时正跟他抱怨我的无奈。那天才他上班的第二天。他说：「这事我来解决。」我说：「行吧孩子，祝你好运。」我说：「加油，继续试。」总之，一天过去，9 点到了。你猜怎么着？思慕雪在晚上 9 点准时送到了，就放在工程师们聚集的站立办公桌上。我尝了尝，是冰的，味道很棒。我当时就想：「天哪，我找到了一个炮管。」后来我几乎把什么都交给他做了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to go back to actually the first question. You shared some amazing advice for how to identify great talent, but I'm still curious, when you find that barrel, for example, when everyone's throwing money at them, there's all these amazing teams to join. What are some things that companies do to attract and convince them to join their team?
turns.zh: 我想回到最开始那个问题。你分享了一些如何识别顶尖人才的绝佳建议，但我还是很好奇：当你找到那个炮管，比如当所有人都在砸钱抢他、有一堆超棒的团队可以加入时，公司会做些什么来吸引并说服他加入自己的团队？

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: The standard of stuff is still true. Mission, selling the vision to mission is indispensable. Most people who have proven talent anyway, at least in the current world, are going to attract offers from multiple opportunities. And so you've got to convince them that your opportunity is very special. (00:23:14): I think one way to do that that's a little bit more nuanced is convince them that their particular skill overlaps with the critical blockers to the current company, meaning they're betting on themselves. So for example, if they are superb at, let's say marketing, if the biggest blocker of the company in the company's current success is not technology, not the product, but we believe it's marketing, it's really easy to go to a world-class marketing person and say, "Not only is this great company building something really cool and interesting that you'll be proud of, but your particular ability is very unique and differentiated and you can solve this." (00:23:55): This is actually how I wound up at Square. Back in 2010, I was actually, I'd just been acquihired into Google and was planning on being a VC actually next after I was investing whenever Google is going to compensate us. And then the investors in Square called me up and they said, "Hey, we've been looking for almost a year now for someone who knows something about financial services yet is still an entrepreneurial." And they're like, "Hey, there's only three of these." At the time, 2010, it was like, "There's only really two or three of you in the world, so would you be interested?" And I said, "Well, maybe." (00:24:33): But that was the argument to me that made me leave Google early after two weeks and infuriate everybody. And bypass Venture for another three years, which had been my plan, was because they made the argument that, hey, I was one of three people in the world that could actually do this job.
turns.zh: 那些基本的东西依然成立。使命、把愿景卖给对方，是不可或缺的。如今这个世界里，大多数已经证明了自己才华的人，都会收到来自多个机会的 offer。所以你必须让他们相信，你的机会非常特别。(00:23:14)：我觉得有一种更微妙的做法是：让他们相信，他们特定的技能，正好与这家公司当前的关键瓶颈重合——也就是说，他们是在为自己下注。比如，如果他们在营销上极其出色，而如果这家公司目前成功的最大瓶颈，不是技术、不是产品，而是我们认为的营销，那你很容易就能对一个世界级的营销人说：「这家伟大的公司不仅在打造让你自豪的、超酷超有趣的东西，而且你特有的能力非常独特、非常有差异化，而你恰恰能解决这个问题。」(00:23:55)：这其实就是我当年加入 Square 的方式。回到 2010 年，我当时刚被 Google 收购并入（acqui-hire），本来计划着在 Google 给我补偿之后，下一步就去当 VC。然后 Square 的投资人给我打电话说：「嘿，我们找快一年了，想找既懂一点金融服务、又还有创业精神的人。」他们说：「嘿，这样的人全世界只有三个。」当时是 2010 年，就像在说：「世界上真正只有两三个你这样的人，所以你感兴趣吗？」我说：「嗯，也许吧。」(00:24:33)：但正是这个理由，让我在 Google 待了两周后就早早离开，把所有人都惹毛了，也让我推迟了三年才去当 VC——那原本是我的计划——因为他们让我相信：嘿，我是全世界仅有的三个真正能干这件事的人之一。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So look, there's a, I don't know if it's ego, but it's also just impact.
turns.zh: 你看，这里有一点点……我不确定这是不是 ego（自我），但也是一种「影响力」的东西。

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: Yep. Well, exactly. Impact, you have talent, you want to use them and you want to feel that you're challenged every day and that what you're doing really, really matters. So I think that can be extremely helpful. (00:25:06): My more important arc in this is I think you have to build a company on undiscovered talent. I don't think you really want to compete for the people that everybody else wants. And I learned this at PayPal. Peter taught me this literally the first week of my job at PayPal, that the way to build a company, we were jogging around the Stanford campuses, you've got to find these undiscovered talent. That's the only way to scale an organization against these large encumbers with infinite money, et cetera. (00:25:34): And I've been on that crusade for 25 years. For those who are interested, you can link to it. I gave a speech at Ramp, how to hire, the talks in detail. I also recommend Eric, CEO of Ramp's speech, which is fairly similar. Both videos are online.
turns.zh: 是的。嗯，没错。影响力——你有才华，你想用它，你想感觉自己每天都在被挑战，而且你做的事真的、真的很重要。所以我认为这一点极其有用。(00:25:06)：但在这方面，我更核心的观点是：我认为你必须在一批「尚未被发现的人才」之上构建公司。我觉得你其实不该去和所有人争抢那些大家都想要的人。这一点是我在 PayPal 学到的。Peter 在我入职 PayPal 第一周就亲自教了我——那时我们在斯坦福校园里慢跑——他说，要搭建一家公司，你必须找到这些尚未被发现的人才。这是你对抗那些资金无限雄厚的庞然大物、并把组织做大的唯一方式。(00:25:34)：25 年来我一直在践行这个信条。有兴趣的人可以去搜相关的链接。我在 Ramp 做过一场关于如何招聘的演讲，讲得很详细。我也推荐 Ramp 的 CEO Eric 的那场演讲，内容相当相似。两个视频都在网上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's such interesting advice and it makes so much sense. You're not going to be able to afford the people that have done the thing at top companies. And also they're just probably not the people to join at early start, right?
turns.zh: 这个建议太有意思了，而且非常在理。你根本负担不起那些在顶级公司已经做成过事的人。而且他们大概也不太会是愿意在很早阶段就加入的人，对吧？

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: Well, they're also not maybe the people you want, so there's adverse election, but it's like a salary cap. Most sports these days have salary caps. And when you're a startup, not only do you have a salary cap, you probably have one 10th the salary cap of the people you're competing with. So you've got to figure out how to leverage less assets to more success.
turns.zh: 嗯，而且他们可能也不是你真正想要的人，所以这里有个逆向选择的问题；但这就像工资帽。如今大多数体育运动都有工资帽。而当你是一家初创公司时，你不仅有工资帽，你的工资帽大概只有你竞争对手的十分之一。所以你必须想清楚，如何用更少的资源撬动更大的成功。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's just one tip when you're looking for undiscovered talent that's a sign of, okay, this person is really special? I know you have a lot to talk about here, but just what's one tip?
turns.zh: 在寻找尚未被发现的人才时，有没有一个信号能说明「好吧，这个人不一般」？我知道这方面你有很多可说的，但就给一个建议好吗？

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: I think it's basically isolating why other people aren't going to process them correctly. Most recruiting at large organizations becomes a homogenous function. And so if you understand why this person is going to get thrown into this black box thing and not get processed accurately, it's pretty easy. (00:26:49): So I always think about, let's say this person was interviewing at Meta or Google or Block these days or Coinbase, what are they going to miss and then why? And then that leads to, oh, perfect. So sometimes it's just lack of information. Sometimes it's controversial to say this, but one of the reasons why the net impact of my higher undiscovered talent is you wind up skewing younger. It's not because you need young people, it's that younger people have, by definition, less data. (00:27:21): It's like we use credit scoring, FICA scores. It's the same thing for employment. By the time you're over 30-some odd things, there's so many data points about you that this black box machine is usually going to process you like many other people. If there's no data points, it's very hard for a black box machine that does homogenous evaluation to evaluate you. So there is alpha, so to speak, by definition for people who have no data points.
turns.zh: 我觉得本质上就是：想清楚为什么其他人不会正确地评估他们。大公司的招聘大多变成了一个同质化的流程。所以只要你能想明白，为什么这个人会被丢进那个「黑盒」里、却得不到准确的评估，事情就简单了。(00:26:49)：所以我总会去想：假设这个人去 Meta、Google、现在的 Block，或者 Coinbase 面试，他们会漏掉什么？为什么会漏掉？然后就会引出：哦，完美。所以有时仅仅是因为信息缺失。有时这么说有点争议，但我大量启用尚未被发现的人才，带来的一个净影响是：你最终会偏向更年轻的人。这不是因为你需要年轻人，而是因为年轻人按定义拥有更少的数据点。(00:27:21)：这就好比我们用信用评分、FICO 分数。雇佣也是一回事。等你过了 30 岁出头，关于你的数据点已经太多了，那个黑盒机器通常会把你和很多其他人一样去处理。如果没有数据点，一个做同质化评估的黑盒机器就很难评估你。所以，对于那些没有任何数据点的人，按定义就存在所谓的「超额收益（alpha）」。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting how this is the same skill as being an investor, picking startups to invest in.
turns.zh: 有意思，这跟做投资人、挑选要投的初创公司，是同一种能力。

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely.
turns.zh: 对，绝对是。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. I want to talk about something else. I asked a few people that know you well that work with you at various companies what to talk to you about. And one person said that when I asked him what to talk about, he said, "My immediate reaction is that he is a bar raiser. No matter what kind of numbers we put up, he pushes us to do more. In fact, often it seems like the better we do, the harder he pushes." Does that resonate?
turns.zh: 好。我想聊点别的。我问过几个在不同公司跟你密切共事、很了解你的人，该跟你聊什么。有个人在我问他聊什么时说：「我第一反应是，他是个『抬高标准的人』（bar raiser）。无论我们交出什么数字，他都逼着我们做得更多。事实上，往往我们做得越好，他逼得越狠。」这说中你了吗？

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: Yeah, I think that's true. I mean, I think, look, ultimately, I'll channel someone else's feedback, but it's in the same vein. So a friend of mine who's a CEO once asked Mike Moore, it's like, "What's the most common denominator of the best CEOs ever?" And he said, "It's the relentless application of force." Quote. (00:28:36): I think that's the job of the CEO. People eventually get comfortable, complacent. The more success you have, the more complacent the organization tends to get, and the single role for the CEO is offsetting that complacency. (00:28:49): So to the point, the more success you have, the better you're doing, the more complacency naturally kicks in. And unless you've erected a network effect, you do not want to get complacent. And even then, debate whether you should. But fundamentally, most businesses are not network-effect businesses. They're not going to run on their own for a long time. (00:29:09): So I think that's one insight is the better you're doing, the more the CEO should push. Secondly, it's a little bit like sports when you're growing up. People, when they're winning, take advantage of feedback better than when they're losing usually. So for example, now what I do is mostly a VC, mostly a board member, mostly a consigliere to a founder. (00:29:36): Maybe what's less intuitive, and you may picked up on this in your research and interviews of people who know me, when a company's struggling, I'm actually usually very non-critical and more like a coach and supporter. Because the company, the founder knows they're struggling. Being critical doesn't really help them solve the problems. That's when being supportive can actually somewhat counterintuitively be more important. But when the company's thriving, it's really important to be critical and isolating things that will eventually be problems while everybody in the company's really happy and borderline complacent. (00:30:12): So you want to be the opposite as a default. And that's like a really good sports coach. When you're winning is when to polish everything and really master the details. When you're losing, you definitely also have to be exciting people and embracing the future and selling the future.
turns.zh: 对，我觉得那是真的。我是说，我觉得——你看，说到底，我引用的是别人的反馈，但方向是一样的。我有个当 CEO 的朋友曾经问 Mike Moore：「史上最优秀的那些 CEO，他们的共同点是什么？」他回答说：「是毫不松懈地施加力量。」原话。(00:28:36)：我认为这就是 CEO 的工作。人最终会变得安逸、自满。你越成功，组织往往就越自满；而 CEO 唯一的作用，就是抵消这种自满。(00:28:49)：所以换言之，你越成功、做得越好，自满就会越自然地滋生。除非你已经建立起了网络效应，否则你绝不该自满。而即便如此，也值得商榷你是否该自满。但从根本上说，大多数生意都不是网络效应生意。它们没法长时间自己运转。(00:29:09)：所以我认为一个洞见是：你做得越好，CEO 就越该往前推。其次，这有点像你成长过程中参与的运动。人在赢的时候，通常比输的时候更能听进反馈。比如，我现在主要做 VC、主要做董事、主要做创始人的军师（consigliere）。(00:29:36)：也许不那么直观的一点是——你在研究和采访了解我的人时可能也发现了——当一家公司陷入困境时，我其实通常很少批评，更像是个教练和支持者。因为公司和创始人都知道自己正陷入困境。批评并不能真正帮他们解决问题。反而是那种支持，在此时能出人意料地更为重要。 但当公司蒸蒸日上时，去做批评、去把那些最终会变成问题的苗头隔离开来，就非常重要——尤其是当公司里所有人都很开心、处于自满边缘的时候。(00:30:12)：所以你默认要做的，恰恰相反。这就像一个真正优秀的体育教练。你赢的时候，才是去打磨一切、真正精通细节的时候。你输的时候，当然也得去激励大家、拥抱未来、兜售未来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So is, say someone's listening, a founder or a product leader, the advice here is just keep pushing harder, set the bar higher as things, even if you're doing great?
turns.zh: 那么，假设有个听众是创始人或产品负责人，你给的建议就是：继续更努力地推，即便你做得已经很好了，也要把标准设得更高？

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: Yeah, if you're doing great. Well, also you have to remember, I remember giving a speech once at Square. It's like you get to a certain threshold, crazy inflection. Momentum gets you to certain valuation and all these attributes. But it's like winning a Super Bowl. The last year was great. Last four quarters was wonderful. It's like winning the Superbowl. You got to come back next year and start your records zero, zero again. And you got to remember that. (00:31:08): Actually, Ventures like that. I'm only as good as my last investment. I've had 13 years or whatever, of pretty damn good investments. But truthfully, I have to wake up every day and find some undiscovered founder that's going to change the world. And if I don't do that, it doesn't matter what I've done in the last 13 years. And a company's like that and the company can skate on autopilot for a while. Venture, you really can't ever skate.
turns.zh: 对，如果你做得很好。嗯，而且你还得记住——我记得在 Square 做过一次演讲——你会到达某个门槛、某个疯狂的拐点。势能把你推到某个估值，带来所有这些光环。但这就像赢下超级碗。去年很棒，过去四个季度很美妙。这就好比赢下超级碗。你明年必须重新回来，战绩归零，从零开始。你得记住这一点。(00:31:08)：其实，风投就是这个道理。我只跟我上一笔投资一样好。我有 13 年、或者随便多少年，相当不错的投资记录。但说实话，我必须每天醒来，去寻找某个能改变世界的、尚未被发现的创始人。如果我不这么做，过去 13 年我做了什么根本不重要。公司也是这样，公司可以在自动驾驶模式上滑行一阵子。但风投，你永远没法靠滑行过日子。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I definitely saw this with Brian Chesky. He just felt like things were going great. And we just shipped amazing products and growth is up and he's just always pedal to the metal no matter what. Just like, "Come on, when are we going to take a little break?" And it's interesting because when we did have little breaks here and there, morales actually went down because people are like, "What am I working on? I don't know. It's not that exciting."
turns.zh: 我在 Brian Chesky 身上绝对看到了这一点。他给人的感觉就是：一切都很顺利。我们刚发布了超棒的产品，增长也在涨，而无论如何他都始终是全力踩油门。我就想：「拜托，我们什么时候能稍微歇一歇？」但有趣的是，当我们这里那里真的歇了歇，士气反而下降了，因为大家会想：「我在做什么？我不知道。这没那么让人兴奋。」

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: Yeah. Brian and I are usually in sync a lot. There's a really good interview when I interviewed him also at the same conference of how to hire, when he talks mostly about founder mode. But I generally subscribe to virtually all of Brian's views. He even taught me some of these things himself. (00:32:08): But the more important point I think you identified, which is very subtle, is really talented people are like superb athletes. And when things are going well and people are really coasting, they're not happy. They have an internal clock tempo. They just want to create things and create value and drive, drive. And the morale actually does go down for the best people in the world when people are skating.
turns.zh: 对。Brian 和我大多数时候都很同步。我在同一场关于如何招聘的会议上采访过他，那次他主要谈的是「创始人模式」（founder mode），那是一段非常好的访谈。但基本上，Brian 的观点我几乎全都认同。有些东西甚至还是他亲自教我的。(00:32:08)：不过，我认为你点出的那个更重要、也更微妙的点是：真正有才华的人就像顶尖运动员。当一切顺利、人们真的在「滑行」（coasting）时，他们并不开心。他们内心有自己的节奏。他们只想去创造东西、创造价值、去驱动、驱动。而当大家在混日子时，世界上最优秀的那批人的士气，确实是在下滑的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So actually along those lines, there's a lot of anxiety in the market, in the job market about the future of careers. Am I going to have a job? Where are things going? And it just feels like people are working very, very hard. They're just putting in a lot of hours, especially the most AI people. It just feels like they're working harder than ever. (00:32:56): I don't know if you saw this thing Tyler Cohen put out of just work harder. Now is the time to work harder because AI is eating away at your value. You probably talked to a lot of people looking for career advice of just like, "This feels scary and I feel like I'm working too hard and what should I do?" I don't know. Do you have any just advice for folks from-
turns.zh: 好。顺着这个话题，就业市场、职业前景里弥漫着大量焦虑。我还会不会有工作？未来会怎样？而且感觉大家都在非常、非常努力地工作。他们投入了大量时间，尤其是那些做 AI 的人。感觉他们比以往任何时候都更拼。(00:32:56)：我不知道你有没有看到 Tyler Cohen 发的那个「就是更努力地工作」。现在就是该更努力的时候，因为 AI 正在侵蚀你的价值。你大概跟很多寻求职业建议的人聊过，他们就像在说：「这感觉很吓人，而且我觉得自己已经工作得太辛苦了，我该怎么办？」我不太确定。你有没有什么建议，给那些……

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: Well, I do think AI is going to radically reorient lots of people's careers, maybe including mine. So I think that's actually true. And I think the way to thrive in a rapidly emerging technology world is to be intellectually curious. So for example, I'm a business person historically. I did actually code when I was really young, but basically professionally, just a business person. What I've noticed in some of the best organizations is the number one consumer of tokens is the CMO-
turns.zh: 嗯，我确实认为 AI 将从根本上重塑很多人的职业生涯，或许也包括我自己的。所以我认为那是真的。而我认为，要在这个快速涌现的技术世界里活得好的方式，是保持求知欲。比如，我历来是个做生意的人。我小时候确实写过代码，但职业生涯里基本上就是个生意人。我在一些最优秀的组织里注意到的一点是：消耗 token 最多的，其实是 CMO——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: CMO.
turns.zh: CMO。

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: ... because these people are intellectually curious. And so they're like, "Wow, there's all these cool things I can do now with my hands. Either I had to rely on other teams or never got access the way I wanted and blah, blah, blah or lag." And they just do it. This is actually true at Opendoor. It's true at another great company that I'm on the board of that's incredible. (00:34:09): And so I think you can be intellectually curious and future-proof yourself more than just, yes, you can work harder and a big subscriber to no days off and working all the time and all that stuff. But fundamentally, the intellectual curiosity is, "I want to learn new things," and that is how you embrace the future.
turns.zh: ……因为这些人有求知欲。所以他们就像在说：「哇，现在我亲手就能做这么多酷炫的事了。以前要么得依赖其他团队，要么就是永远拿不到我想要的权限，要么就是滞后。」然后他们就直接自己干了。在 Opendoor 这确实是真的。在我担任董事的另一家很厉害的公司里也是真的。(00:34:09)：所以我认为，你可以靠求知欲来给自己「未来-proof」，而不仅仅只是——是的，你可以更努力地工作，我也是「不放假、一直工作」那一套的忠实信徒。但从根本上说，求知欲是「我想学新东西」，而这就是你拥抱未来的方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And you said CMO is who's the most-
turns.zh: 你刚说 CMO 是消耗 token 最多的——

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: CMO. In both of these two companies-
turns.zh: CMO。在这两家公司里——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So interesting.
turns.zh: 太有意思了。

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: ... both massive, awesome companies with lots of engineers. And I think that's very encouraging. For the executive particularly, like, "This is definitely the best executive in the company."
turns.zh: ……这两家都是体量巨大、很棒、拥有大量工程师的公司。我认为这非常鼓舞人心。尤其对高管来说，就像在说：「这绝对是公司里最优秀的高管。」

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And what are they building? Is it landing pages and paid tests?
turns.zh: 那他们到底在构建什么？是落地页和付费测试吗？

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: Well, sometimes it's more like what we would've thought of analytics. Sometimes it's actually campaigns, actual campaigns. It's just like they don't need to rely upon deputies and deputies and deputies to get actual work product. And so they're just shipping things or shipping drafts of things or giving the CEO insights into things themselves.
turns.zh: 嗯，有时更像是我们会归类为分析的东西。有时其实是真正的营销活动、实际的 campaign。就是他们不再需要层层依赖副手才能拿到真正的工作成果。所以他们就直接交付东西、交付东西的草稿，或者亲自给 CEO 提供洞察。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to get your take on the future of specifically the product triad. You work with a lot of product people, engineers, designers. Everyone's always wondering, what the hell is going to happen in my career? Thoughts on just the future of those three specific roles?
turns.zh: 我想听听你对「产品三件套」（product triad）未来的看法。你跟很多产品人、工程师、设计师共事。大家总是在想，我的职业生涯到底会怎样？就这三者具体角色的未来，你有什么想法？

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: Well, I saw this podcast or I listened to this podcast that Peter Fenn did. And he convinced me that the idea of a PM makes no sense basically in the future. If you think about decomposing the logic is what does PM usually do? They take these inputs from customers, they create this sequential roadmap that's well organized over the next year, blah, blah, blah, blah, blah. (00:35:52): That world is ridiculous. Right now, the capabilities of foundation models or companies like Lovable and things like that are just so improving such a rapid rate that it makes no sense to have a year-long roadmap. And they're just incoherent. There are things that were impossible to do in November that are actually pretty easy to do right now in March. And so I think you need to build an organization that's incredibly adept at, people say nimble and all that stuff, but incredibly adept at changing the roadmap almost on the fly. (00:36:31): And I think intermediaries like conventional PMs don't make a lot of sense versus being prepared intellectually, embracing and exploding, noticing. So someone needs to notice that, "Oh, wow, we can actually do this." But then exploiting it this week is the future of a high growth stellar startup. We'll notice that something's now possible this week and create new features and new value for customers next week.
turns.zh: 嗯，我看到、或者说我听了一期 Peter Fenn 做的播客。他让我相信：基本上，未来产品经理这个概念已经没有意义了。如果你去拆解一下逻辑——PM 通常都在做什么？他们从客户那里拿输入，做出一份未来一年排得井井有条的 sequential roadmap， blah blah blah blah blah。(00:35:52)：那个世界很荒谬。如今，基础模型或者 Lovable 这类公司的能力，正以如此快的速度提升，搞个长达一年的 roadmap 根本没意义。而且它们本身就不连贯。有些在 11 月还不可能做到的事，到了今年 3 月其实已经相当容易了。所以我认为，你需要搭建一个极其擅长——人们总说 nimble（灵活）之类的——但极其擅长近乎实时地改变 roadmap 的组织。(00:36:31)：而我认为，像传统 PM 这样的中间人，意义已经不大了，取而代之的是在智识上做好准备、去拥抱和引爆、去察觉。所以，需要有人去察觉：「哦哇，我们现在其实能做到这个了。」然后在本周就把它利用起来——这就是高增长的明星初创公司的未来。我们会在本周注意到某件事现在可行了，并在下周为客户创造出新功能和新价值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's such an interesting area of discussion. A lot of people listening to this RPM. So I want to try to defend that role just to see if I can convince you otherwise. And by the way, I will say Mark Andreessen had this really good visual of just what's happening here is all those three functions, it's like the standoff where they're all like, "I'm good taking... The future is my role. The future is design, that's engineering is the future." (00:37:22): So the way I see it is as AI makes it easier to build and eats the middle of the software development process, just anyone can build detailed AI, here's what I want. The hard part, the gap at least for now is figuring out what to build and then aligning everyone around what to build.
turns.zh: 这是个很有意思的讨论领域。很多听这期播客的人……所以我想试着为这个角色辩护一下，看看能不能把你说服。顺便说，Mark Andreessen 有个很好的可视化，讲的就是这里发生的事——那三个职能就像对峙一样，他们都在说：「我擅长的才是未来。设计的未来、工程的未来……」(00:37:22)：所以我的看法是：随着 AI 让构建变得更容易、并吃掉软件开发流程的中间环节，既然任何人都能构建细节化的 AI，「我想要的」这部分就在这里。难的、至少目前还是缺口的部分，是搞清楚要构建什么，然后让所有人就「构建什么」对齐。

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: I agree with that. I actually think whether you talk about someone who used to be a PM or someone who used to be a designer or called an engineer, the skill is more like being a CEO now, which is what are we building and why?
turns.zh: 我同意这点。我其实认为，无论你说的是曾经是 PM 的人、曾经是设计师的人，还是被称为工程师的人，现在这种能力更像是当一名 CEO——也就是我们到底在构建什么、为什么？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: And to be a successful engineer, that trait's critical, to be a successful designer. Because the tools and the ability to actually create the thing, an object, is going to be easier and easier. But the art is knowing what to build. (00:38:07): Another competitor of mine, Alfred Lin at Sequoia likes to talk about being a chef. When you're a chef at a prime restaurant, you're not actually cooking the dish. You're sampling your colleagues and editing their work a little bit, but fundamentally, it's half a commercial role. (00:38:26): Being a chef at a famous restaurant is what's our value proposition? How do we differentiate ourselves? How do we brand ourselves? What's our segment? What's our pricing, et cetera? What's our location even? That's what makes a famous chef. It's not they're literally cooking the dish all the time.
turns.zh: 而要成为一名成功的工程师，那个特质很关键；要成为一名成功的设计师也是。因为真正去创造那个东西、那个实物的工具和能力，会越来越容易。但艺术在于知道该构建什么。(00:38:07)：我的一个竞争对手，Sequoia 的 Alfred Lin 喜欢用「当主厨」来打比方。当你在一家顶级餐厅当主厨时，你其实并不是在做那道菜。你是在品鉴同事们的出品、稍微编辑一下他们的工作，但从根本上说，那是一半商业角色。(00:38:26)：在知名餐厅当主厨，我们的价值主张是什么？我们如何差异化？我们如何做品牌？我们的细分市场是什么？我们的定价是多少，等等？甚至我们的选址在哪？那才是成就一位名厨的东西。并不是他们时刻都在亲自掌勺做菜。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. I 100% agree. Interestingly enough, PMs are called mini CEOs often. And I think the important thing is it's not like, what do you call this person? I think the question is what skill will be most ... Where are human brains still going to be necessary? And it's-
turns.zh: 好。我 100% 同意。有意思的是，PM 常被称为「迷你 CEO」。而我认为重要的是：问题不在于你怎么称呼这个人。我认为真正的问题是，哪项技能将是最……人类的大脑在哪些地方仍然不可或缺？而在于——

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: Business acumen. It's basically business acumen.
turns.zh: 商业敏锐度。本质上就是商业敏锐度（business acumen）。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Right. What will help this company grow and succeed-
turns.zh: 对。什么能帮这家公司增长和成功——

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... and win?
turns.zh: ……并取胜？

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: I understand the company's business equation, where we're trying to go and what the inputs and connection outputs are. And I can, on my own, create things that move the needle or potentially move the needle. It's very exciting because you can actually drive impact much more easily now as an individual.
turns.zh: 我理解这家公司的商业方程式——我们要去哪里、输入和连接输出分别是什么。而我能够靠自己，创造出能推动指针、或者可能推动指针的东西。这非常令人兴奋，因为现在作为一个个体，你能真正容易得多地驱动影响力了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: My conclusion based on what you just shared is of the three roles, which role is best at that? And historically, it'd be PMs. Obviously, I think the important thing here is it's great PMs or great engineers, designers will do well. But I think interestingly, what you're describing to me is what it sounds like what a great PM would be really good at basically represents [inaudible 00:39:41]
turns.zh: 基于你刚才分享的，我的结论是：在这三个角色里，哪个角色最擅长这件事？历史上来说，会是 PM。显然，我认为重要的是——优秀的 PM、优秀的工程师、设计师都会做得很好。但我觉得有意思的是，你向我描述的，听起来就像是一个优秀 PM 真正擅长的事，基本上就代表了 [听不清 00:39:41]

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: If they were exceptional, I think that's right. But I think a lot of the best engineers I've worked with have commercial instincts like Max Levchin has this on steroids. Jeremy Stoppelman, he's worked with me very closely at PayPal before he started Yelp and got promoted to be engineering director and vice president of PayPal, had commercial instincts back when he was an individual contributor. So I think there are great engineers who are technically proficient that have always understood the business building.
turns.zh: 如果他们出类拔萃，我认为那是对的。但我认为，我共事过很多最优秀的工程师，都有着商业本能——就像 Max Levchin 在这点上做到了极致。Jeremy Stoppelman 在创办 Yelp 之前，曾和我非常密切地在 PayPal 共事，并被提拔为工程总监和 PayPal 副总裁，他在还是独立贡献者的时候，就已经有商业本能了。所以我认为，有很多技术过硬的伟大的工程师，一直以来都理解「做生意、建公司」这件事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I think that's the ultimate unicorn is an engineer that is also very business-minded.
turns.zh: 对。我认为那种终极独角兽，就是一个同时也极具商业头脑的工程师。

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: It's going to put a premium. I think this is what ... The age of AI will put an incredible premium on that because they're not going to need a large team. You're not going to be marshaling the forces. (00:40:25): Another example is a good friend of mine is director of engineering at Ramp. He ships as much code personally. So he has a team of about 20 people. He personally ships as much code as he used to as an individual contributor while he's managing a team of 20 because the tools are so great and he's become a leading pioneer in the usage of AI. (00:40:47): And he's basically using AI as a second team. He's basically like, "Okay, you're the team manager. You do this, you do this, you do this, this, this together, check this out, blah, blah, blah." And I think that is definitely the future.
turns.zh: 这会获得极高的溢价。我认为……AI 时代会给这种人极高的溢价，因为他们不需要一支庞大的团队。你不再需要去调度大军。(00:40:25)：另一个例子是我的一位好朋友，他在 Ramp 担任工程总监。他个人交付的代码量，跟以前当独立贡献者时一样多。他管着大约 20 人的团队。他能亲自交付和以前当 IC 时一样多的代码，同时还在管理 20 人的团队——因为工具太好了，而且他已经成为使用 AI 的领军先锋。(00:40:47)：他基本上把 AI 当成了第二支团队。他大概就像在说：「好，你是团队经理。你做这个，你做这个，你做这个、这个、这个，一起搞，检查一下这个，blah blah blah。」而我认为，那绝对就是未来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I 100% agree. Engineers that are very good at that are just extra valuable. What's your take on design in the future of design, the value of design?
turns.zh: 我 100% 同意。极其擅长这一点的工程师，就是额外地有价值。你对设计的未来、设计的价值，有什么看法？

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: Well, it's interesting. Design and code are merging. And it's not clear to me who triumphs of is it code becomes design? And design just translate automatically into code. I've made some investments that bet on both in some ways, but I think they're merging in a way where they're not separate fiefdoms anymore.
turns.zh: 嗯，这很有意思。设计和代码正在融合。而我并不清楚谁会胜出——是代码变成了设计？还是设计会自动翻译成代码？我在某些方面对两边都下过注，但我认为它们正在以这样一种方式融合：它们不再是彼此分割的领地了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I am so excited to tell you about this season's supporting sponsor Vanta. Vanta helps over 15,000 companies like Cursor, Ramp, Duolingo, Snowflake, and Atlassian earn and prove trust with their customers. Teams are building and shipping products faster than ever thanks to AI. But as a result, the amount of risk being introduced into your product and your business is higher than it's ever been. (00:41:58): Every security leader that I talk to is feeling the increasing weight of protecting their organization, their business, and not to mention their customer data. Because things are moving so fast, they are constantly reacting, having to guess at priorities, and having to make do with outdated solutions. (00:42:15): Vanta automates compliance and risk management with over 35 security and privacy frameworks, including SOC 2, ISO 27001, and HIPAA. This helps companies get compliant, fast, and stay compliant. More than ever before, trust has the power to make or break your business. Learn more at vanta.com/lenny. And as a listener of this podcast, you get $1,000 off Vanta. That's vanta.com/lenny. (00:42:42): What I'm seeing is something really interesting happening with design. On the one hand, I just did some analysis on the job market for design. And it's basically plateaued in terms of the number of open design roles over the past three years, just hasn't gone anywhere. It's flat. (00:42:55): We had the head of Claude design, Jenny Wen, on the podcast, and she had this insight that the design process ... There's no time for the traditional design process. There's like engineers are shipping 17 things a day. There's no time to sit there and help mock and prototype and all these things.
turns.zh: 我非常兴奋地要跟你说说本季的支持赞助商 Vanta。Vanta 帮助超过 15,000 家公司——比如 Cursor、Ramp、Duolingo、Snowflake 和 Atlassian——赢得并证明其客户对他们的信任。得益于 AI，团队打造和交付产品的速度比以往任何时候都快。但与此同时，注入到你产品和你业务中的风险量，也比以往任何时候都高。(00:41:58)：每一个我聊过的安全负责人，都感受到保护其组织、其业务、更别提客户数据的沉重压力。因为事情发展得太快，他们总是在被动反应，不得不去猜测优先级，并且只能用过时方案将就。(00:42:15)：Vanta 用超过 35 个安全和隐私框架（包括 SOC 2、ISO 27001 和 HIPAA）自动化合规与风险管理。这帮公司快速达到合规，并保持合规。信任比以往任何时候都更有能力成就或毁掉你的业务。前往 vanta.com/lenny 了解更多。作为本播客的听众，你能省下 Vanta 的 1,000 美元。就是 vanta.com/lenny。(00:42:42)：我所看到的是，设计领域正发生一件真正有意思的事。一方面，我刚做了一些关于设计就业市场的分析。过去三年里，开放的设计岗位数量基本是持平的——哪儿也没去，是平的。(00:42:55)：我们请过 Claude 的设计负责人 Jenny Wen 上节目，她有一个洞见：设计流程……传统设计流程已经没有时间了。工程师一天能交付 17 个东西。根本没时间坐在那儿做 mock、做原型，以及所有这些事。

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: Well, let me give you a couple of concrete examples. So at Shopify, the way they develop, they've been doing this for over two years now. So this may seem normal, but they have not let PMs provide PowerPoint or keynote presentations on product for two years. Every presentation on product has to be a workable demo, and they just expect the PMs to create the products. And the execs just refuse to look at static, "We're going to have this feature." No, I want everything working. This is for two years. So I think that, again, everything's just merging together.
turns.zh: 好，让我给你几个具体的例子。在 Shopify，他们的开发方式——这已经做了两年多了。所以这可能看起来正常，但他们已经有两年没让 PM 用 PowerPoint 或 Keynote 来做产品演示了。每一个产品相关的演示，都必须是可运行的 demo，而且他们就期望 PM 去把产品做出来。高管们干脆拒绝看静态的东西——「我们要有这个功能了。」不，我要一切都能跑起来。这已经持续两年了。所以我认为，这又一次说明，一切都在融合。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's so interesting. You would think though, because there are so many products launching every single day, there's just endless things to pay attention to, you would think design would be a differentiator more and more.
turns.zh: 这太有意思了。你可能会想，既然每天都有那么多产品发布，有那么多东西值得关注，你可能会以为设计会越来越成为差异化因素。

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: I do agree with that. I do agree with that actually. I think the alpha is in design just like in marketing. It's not the tools, it's not the channels, not the metrics. It's the storytelling. It's how do you cut through the clutter in the snappiest, most compelling, possible way? It's an NP problem. There's so many different words you can use to express the same concept, but the person who can say, "This is the way to frame it," the proverbial 1,000 songs in your market, is worth all the tools in the world.
turns.zh: 我确实同意这点。我其实是同意的。我认为设计里的 alpha（超额收益），就跟营销里一样。不在于工具，不在于渠道，不在于指标。在于讲故事。在于你如何以最利落、最打动人的方式，穿透那些噪音？这是个 NP 问题。表达同一个概念，你能用的词有千千万万，但那个能说出「这就是该有的框架」的人——正所谓你市场里那 1,000 首歌——值得世界上所有的工具。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. So that's the other part of my insight recently is just as AI makes it easier to build, it's kind of expanding from the middle out. And what remains is figuring out what to build and making iterating on the idea. And then it's at the other end of the spectrum, which is distribution, getting anyone to pay any attention to what the heck you've done, because again, there's so much happening every single day.
turns.zh: 对。所以这是我最近另一个洞见的另一半：随着 AI 让构建变容易，它有点像是从中间向外扩张。而留存下来的，是搞清楚要构建什么、并对想法做迭代。然后是在光谱的另一端——也就是分发，让任何人哪怕稍微关注一下你到底做了什么，因为再说一次，每天发生的事实在太多了。

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: Yeah. Cutting through the clutter. I mean, that's always been critical. I mean, when people are pitching me as an investor, it's one of the things I'm dialing into immediately is how the hell is this going to cut through the clutter? It's one of the reasons why I don't like to take customer feedback into account because by definition, when you put something in front of a customer, that's not a proxy for the real world. (00:45:09): In the real world, you have to cut through the clutter while they're going to their Barry's bootcamp, while they're doing their job, while they're raising their kids, et cetera, et cetera, while they're walking, while they're on the subway. An isolated fake experiment doesn't give you actionable insights and often is directionally wrong.
turns.zh: 对。穿透噪音。我是说，那一直都至关重要。我的意思是，当人们作为投资人向我 pitch 时，这是我立刻就会 dial in（聚焦）的事情之一：这玩意儿到底要怎么穿透噪音？这也是为什么我不喜欢把客户反馈纳入考量——因为按定义，当你把东西摆到一个客户面前，那并不是真实世界的代理。(00:45:09)：在真实世界里，你得在他们去 Barry's bootcamp（健身课）的路上、在他们工作的时候、在抚养孩子的时候，等等等等，在他们散步的时候、在地铁上的时候，穿透那些噪音。一个孤立的虚假实验，给不了你可执行的洞察，而且常常在方向上就是错的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interestingly on that line, there's a few companies that are launching, Simile is one, that is simulating humans. I don't know if you heard about this company. They basically are building AI models of the actual people so that you can simulate your marketing launch and your product experience with people before you launch.
turns.zh: 顺着这条线，有个有意思的点：有几家正在 launch 的公司，Simile 是其中一家，它在模拟人类。我不知道你听没听过这家公司。他们基本上是在构建真实人类的 AI 模型，这样你就能在正式发布前，用这些「人」去模拟你的营销发布和产品体验。

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: I don't know if I've seen that specific company. I have seen one or two pitches. My general question as a refrain on those type of companies is what are they training on? Because again, if they're not training on the right data, it's dangerous to say you're simulating humans.
turns.zh: 我不确定我有没有见过那家具体的公司。我见过一两个类似的 pitch。对于这类公司，我一贯的疑问是：他们拿什么来训练？因为再说一次，如果他们不是用正确的数据训练，那么说自己在「模拟人类」是很危险的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. That is the question. Oh, man. What a weird world. Along these lines, actually, you have this, I don't know if you call it a hot take that AI content is going to surpass human content and that's just the future.
turns.zh: 对。对。那就是问题所在。哦天哪。这世界真怪。顺着这个话题，其实你有一个——我不确定你管这叫不叫「热观点」——就是 AI 内容将会超越人类内容，而那只是未来。

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: Oh, that's inevitable.
turns.zh: 哦，那是必然的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was talking to someone and then she was saying in the Chinese TikTok app, it's just all AI videos now and it's very good. She actually enjoys watching these videos and these stories.
turns.zh: 我刚在跟一个人聊，然后她说，在中国的 TikTok（抖音）应用里，现在全都是 AI 视频了，而且做得非常好。她其实很享受看这些视频和这些故事。

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: I think there'd be a binary sort maybe. I could see products and content thriving that is clearly still human-generated and that there's some desire for authenticity. Just like, for example, this piece of art is a Warhol. Anybody could create this now, high fidelity, but there's still an appreciation for this was created by Andy Warhol. (00:46:51): I think there's going to be a curated experience with a premium of provenance that you know is human-created. And then there's just going to be a rank filtering of what's the best content and whether it's AI-generated or not. It's a little bit like the Ben Thompson strategy thing of curation versus algorithm. There's going to be two polls and the curation may be for human created stuff. And then there's going to be the algorithm, which is just what's the best?
turns.zh: 我认为可能会出现一种二元分野。我能想象，那些明确仍然由人类生成的产品和内容会蓬勃发展，而且存在某种对「真实性」的渴望。就像，比如，这件艺术品是 Warhol（沃霍尔）的。现在任何人都能高保真地创造它，但对「这是 Andy Warhol 创作的」这件事，仍然存在欣赏。(00:46:51)：我认为，会出现一种带有「溯源溢价」的策展式体验——你知道它是人类创作的。然后另一种就是纯粹的筛选过滤：什么是最好的内容，无论它是不是 AI 生成的。这有点像 Ben Thompson 关于「策展 vs 算法」的战略论述。会出现两个阵营，而策展可能面向人类创作的东西。然后就是算法那一端——也就是到底什么最好？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I 100% believe that. That makes so much sense. I was just thinking the other day, it's so interesting that AI is getting very good at video. Videos are actually fun to watch that are AI-generated. And then images are getting really good, but writing is still really bad that is AI-generated. And it's ironic that it's called a large language model. It's all context, text, text trained. And it's just like that's the thing it's least good at, which is really weird.
turns.zh: 我 100% 相信这一点。这太有道理了。我前两天刚在想，AI 在视频上变得非常好，这事儿真有意思。AI 生成的视频其实挺好看。然后图像也变得真的很好，但写作仍然是 AI 生成里非常糟糕的部分。而讽刺的是，它叫「大语言模型」。它全是上下文、文本、文本训练出来的。而它最不擅长的，恰恰就是这件事，这真的很怪。

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: Well, I think part of that's an economic decision of token rationing by the LLMs. They basically are, when you prompt, they're trying to make their economics work within a bell curve distribution. And so for example, if you prompt an LLM to write something that's very short, the quality is significantly better than if it's a page to chapter to book. I think it's tokening ratioing versus actual quality.
turns.zh: 嗯，我认为那部分原因是 LLM 在 token 上做了经济性的配给（rationing）。它们基本上，当你 prompt 时，是在一个钟形曲线的分布内，试图让它们的经济模型成立。所以举个例子，如果你让一个 LLM 写非常短的东西，质量会明显好于让它写一页、一章、一本书。我认为那是 token 的配比问题，而不是真实的质量问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You would think though, I don't know if it was Hemmingway of just like, "If I had more time, I would've made it shorter." It's more work. Yeah.
turns.zh: 你可能会想，不过，我不知道这是不是海明威说的——就像：「如果我时间更多，我本可以把文章写得更短。」那是更费工夫的。对。

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: But then you have ... I think the writing, right now what works best is short, many short examples and then-
turns.zh: 但然后你会有……我认为现在写作效果最好的是：短的、很多短的例子，然后——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Tweets, basically.
turns.zh: 推文，基本上。

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: ... picking, editing, reprompting. It's a little bit like when I used to be a litigator 25 plus years ago, the hardest part of writing a brief or all the art and all the magic was the first paragraph. If I could write that first paragraph really well, the chance I would win the case and convince the judge would go through the roof. (00:48:55): So what I would actually do is I might have three weeks to write a brief. I might spend the first week or more walking around the office, thinking through, "How am I going to nail the first three sentences?" Once I figured out how I wanted to frame those first three sentences, I could write 30 pages in two days, but getting that right could take a week or two. (00:49:20): Sometimes it would occur to me in the shower or literally the shower or in the middle of a run. It's like, "Oh my God, here's how I distill it." Then I could just sit down and power through the rest of the brief. And I think it's a little bit like that. The powering through the rest of the brief works well, you still need the first three sentences.
turns.zh: ……挑选、编辑、重新 prompt。这有点像我 25 年多前当诉讼律师的时候——写一份案情摘要（brief）最难、也最见功力与魔力的部分，是第一段。如果我能把第一段写得非常好，我赢下案子、说服法官的几率就会飙升。(00:48:55)：所以我实际会这么做：我可能有三周时间来写一份 brief。我可能会花第一周甚至更久，在办公室里走来走去，思考：「我要怎么把头三句话钉死？」一旦我想清楚要怎么框定那头三句话，我就能在两天内写出 30 页，但把那部分想对，可能要花上一两周。(00:49:20)：有时它会在我洗澡时、真的就是洗澡时、或者在一次跑步中途冒出来。就像：「哦天哪，原来我是这么把它提炼出来的。」然后我就能坐下来，一鼓作气把 brief 的剩下部分写完。我认为这有点像那件事。一鼓作气写完剩下部分效果很好，但你仍然需要那头三句话。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there a story from that time in your life that would be interesting to share? I didn't even know about that.
turns.zh: 那段经历里，有没有什么有趣的故事可以分享？我之前都不知道这回事。

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: So yeah, not everybody knows. I spent the first four and a half years of my professional career as a law clerk and then litigator, which occasionally comes in handy truthfully. Sometimes trading off business risk against legal risk is a valuable thing to do. Sometimes it's not accidental that many of my best investments are in financial services in heavily regulated areas because I think I can sort of do the legal risk assessment in my own brain. This was definitely true back in the day when I invested in YouTube. But I think most things that lawyers learn are very inconsistent with being entrepreneur. (00:50:19): So when you're graded as a lawyer, you learn every exam in law school virtually is issue spotting. So you get credit for identify ... There's fact patterns and identify all the issues and then resolve them. So you learn to identify everything that can go wrong, moderately useful, but very not useful as an entrepreneur. (00:50:39): I mean, sure, you can identify all the reasons a company could fail, not that difficult to do. The art is solving those. So not the best training. And then you also measure your productivity by hours worked. Literally, you bill per hour. It took me two years, maybe a year and a half after converting to technology to stop tracking all my time. I used to literally write down in my notebook, "Oh, half hour of this meeting, 20 minutes on this, blah, blah, blah." I just couldn't get that out of my brain.
turns.zh: 对，不是所有人都知道。我职业生涯的头四年半，是当法律助理，然后是诉讼律师，这一点偶尔还真派上用场。有时把商业风险和法律风险做权衡，是件有价值的事。有时，我一些最成功的投资是在监管很重的金融服务领域，这并非偶然——因为我认为我能在自己的大脑里做法律风险评估。当年我投资 YouTube 时，这绝对是真的。但我认为，律师学的绝大多数东西，和当创业者是非常不一致的。(00:50:19)：你在法学院几乎每场考试考的都是「找问题点」（issue spotting）。所以你会因为识别出……有事实模式、找出所有问题、然后去解决它们而得分。所以你学会识别一切可能出错的地方——有点用，但对创业者来说非常没用。(00:50:39)：我是说，当然，你能识别出一家公司可能失败的所有理由，那并不难。艺术在于解决它们。所以这不是最好的训练。而且你还会按工作小时数来衡量自己的生产力。字面上，你按小时计费。我转行做科技之后，花了两年、也许一年半，才不再追踪自己所有的时间。我以前真的会在笔记本上写：「哦，这个会半小时，那个事 20 分钟，blah blah blah。」我就是没法把那套从脑子里去掉。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is so funny. And David Sachs was a lawyer too. It's interesting.
turns.zh: 太好笑了。而且 David Sachs 也是律师出身。真有意思。

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: That's true. Peter was a lawyer.
turns.zh: 那是真的。Peter 也是律师。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Peter too.
turns.zh: Peter 也是。

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: Peter was smart enough to quit after five months and four days, I think. David never practiced so maybe even smarter than both of us.
turns.zh: Peter 够聪明，在五个月零四天之后就 quit 了，我想是。David 从来没真正执业过，所以也许比我们俩都更聪明。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. I'm going to hit on some hot takes, contrarian takes that you have. You have a number of these. I heard you share on a podcast recently. They asked you, "Why don't you have as many contrarian takes these days?" And you're like, "Well, they've just all been proven right."
turns.zh: 好。我要聊几个你有的「热观点」、反共识观点。你有一堆这样的。我听说你最近在播客上分享过。他们问你：「为什么你这些天没那么多反共识观点了？」然后你说：「嗯，因为它们现在统统都被证明是对的。」

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: And that's the problem is if you have good ideas, eventually you want them to be adopted. It's a little bit like when you're an investor, you want to be contrarian. So Airbnb, you start with a contrarian take, but eventually if the company's going to succeed, it has to become consensus. Everybody in the world has to use it and believe in it and trust it. So you want that inflection. You don't want to just have contrarian takes and then nobody believe it. So you do need a refresh rate. And then the question is, how do you find new ideas? But you want to actually exhaust them.
turns.zh: 而问题就在于：如果你有好想法，你最终会希望它们被采纳。这有点像你当投资人时，你想反共识。所以 Airbnb，你从一个反共识观点起步，但最终如果这家公司要成功，它必须变成共识。全世界的人都得用它、相信它、信任它。所以你要的是那个拐点。你不是只想守着反共识观点、然后没人信它。所以你确实需要「刷新率」。然后问题就是，你怎么找到新想法？但你确实想把旧的耗尽。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So one that I think people still just would disagree with is that your advice is for, unless you're building an enterprise company, you don't actually want to be talking to customers.
turns.zh: 好。那么有一个，我认为人们到现在都还会不同意的观点是：你的建议是——除非你在做一家企业级公司，否则你其实根本不该去跟客户交谈。

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: Yeah, I hate talking to customers. I refuse to allow colleagues about and talk to customers. You can talk with the famous stuff and the Steve Jobs, the horses and the faster horses and all this stuff. But I think it's more important is it's often directionally wrong. Customers don't know what they want and they're very bad because it's a subconscious decision, especially for consumers. What I purchase, what I wear is not a conscious decision. And when you're consciously trying to answer a subconscious decision, you actually give misleading information even when you're trying. (00:52:53): The proverbial example I like to use, but it's instructive is ask anybody who drives a super fancy car like a Porsche or a Lamborghini, why they bought the car. 99% of the time they will tell you every reason except the real reason. Once you realize that, you're like, "I'm never asking customers anything." (00:53:10): Now, a hardcore enterprise, customer development does work because there is a decision maker. And the decision maker is mostly making utilitarian decision. And yes, there's political forces within the organization and you may or may not be able to tap into those, but fundamentally, extracting that information is valuable, but a consumer, SMB, micro-emergent product, unmitigated disaster.
turns.zh: 对，我讨厌跟客户交谈。我也拒绝让同事去跟客户交谈。你可以拿那些有名的东西说事，比如 Steve Jobs、比如「用户想要更快的马」那一套。但我认为更重要的是：它在方向上常常就是错的。客户不知道自己想要什么，而且——尤其是消费者——因为那是潜意识里的决定，他们做得很糟。我买什么、穿什么，都不是有意识的决定。而当你有意识地试图去回答一个潜意识的决定时，即便你努力想答好，给出的也是误导性的信息。(00:52:53)：我喜欢的、也很有启发性的那个老生常谈的例子是：去问任何开超跑（比如保时捷或兰博基尼）的人，为什么买这辆车。99% 的情况下，他们会告诉你每一个理由，除了真正的那个。一旦你意识到这一点，你就会想：「我永远不再问客户任何事了。」(00:53:10)：现在，对于硬核的企业级客户，客户开发确实是管用的，因为那里有个决策者。而决策者大多做的是功利性的决定。是的，组织内部有政治力量，你可能、也可能没法触达那些，但从根本上说，把那类信息提取出来是有价值的；但如果是消费者、中小企业、微型新兴产品，那就是一场彻头彻尾的灾难。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so the implication here is you need to rely on your instincts and gut and experience.
turns.zh: 所以这里的含义是：你需要依赖自己的本能、直觉和经验。

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: Yeah. I mean, humans are humans. I have this other line I like, which is everything important you need to learn about humans was written by Shakespeare. Just read Shakespeare. That's better than all the customer research. (00:53:52): Now you are producing a movie and ultimately, this movie doesn't just need to be critically acclaimed. You have to sell tickets. So if you're not selling tickets, you have to question, "Okay, is the trailer wrong? Is our distribution where we're trying to meet people to let them know about the movie, is that wrong?" (00:54:14): Fortunately, unlike a movie, you can go back and say, "Have I casted this somewhat incorrectly? Is the script slightly off," et cetera? But the goal is selling tickets and that's what you want to optimize for. But if you don't sell tickets successfully, economically, efficiently, you definitely want to go back in a loop and try to reorient things so that you are selling tickets.
turns.zh: 对。我是说，人就是人。我还有另一句喜欢的话，就是：关于人类，所有你需要学习的重要东西，莎士比亚都写过了。去读莎士比亚就行。那比所有客户研究都强。(00:53:52)：现在你在制作一部电影，而归根结底，这部电影不能只是获得评论界的好评。你得卖票。所以如果你卖不出票，你就得问：「好，是预告片错了？我们试图接触到观众、让他们知道这部电影的分发渠道，错了？」(00:54:14)：幸运的是，跟电影不同，你可以回过头来说：「我是不是在某些地方选角选错了？剧本是不是稍微偏了？」等等。但目标是卖票，而那才是你想要优化的东西。但如果你没能成功、高效、经济地卖出票，你绝对该回到循环里，试着重新调整，好让你在卖票。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So this is like CAC LTB kind of stuff is what I'm hearing here. And so your insight here is just, it's not going to help you. You're saying moreso it's actually harmful.
turns.zh: 所以这听起来就像 CAC、LTV 那类东西，是我在你这儿听到的。而你的洞见是：它帮不了你。你更想说的是，它实际上是有害的。

turns.speaker: Keith Rabois
turns.en: It's harmful.
